title: 1.1 · Every riser in the flight
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.1 · Every riser in the flight

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can measure a repeated dimension across a run, describe the spread, and sketch what I measured.MEASURE 40 · DRAW 40 · HAND IT OVER 30☐ Tapes, one each ☐ Clipboards ☐ Stair access ☐ Board
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Go to the stair. No preamble. Every student measures every riser in one flight, top to bottom, and writes each one down in order. Then the treads.RememberPrior knowledge · d=0.41
15–40

Back in the room, all the numbers go on the board. They will not agree with each other and — more importantly — the risers will not agree with EACH OTHER. Find the biggest and the smallest in the flight. Subtract. That number goes in a box on the board and stays there.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Is that spread you, or is it the stair? How would we tell those apart?”

AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
40–80

Sketch the flight in section — freehand, no straightedge. Proportions first. Then put your riser numbers on it, in order.

ELL/SWD: sketch the shape with no numbers at all first, then add them in a second pass.

ApplyCooperative learning · d=0.55
80–110Trade sketches. Could the other person build this flight from your drawing? Count the questions they have to ask.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The spread between the biggest and smallest riser is the number that matters. Do not tell them there is a code limit and do not tell them what it is. That is the hook and it stays open until 3.1.

Separating “my measuring varies” from “the stair varies” is the Unit 1 repeatability target doing real work. Anyone who measures the same riser twice and gets two answers has found their own contribution.

MATERIALS & PREP

MEASURE THE FLIGHT YOURSELF FIRST. You need to know the real spread before you send twenty students at it. If the flight is dead even, pick a different one — an older wing, an exterior stair, a basement flight.

Confirm you can hold twenty students in a stairwell for a class period. If you cannot: bleacher steps in the fieldhouse work, so does any exterior stair, so does a single flight taken in two groups while the other half sketches.

One tape per student, and clipboards. Numbers recorded on the stair beat numbers remembered on the walk back.

TEACHER NOTES

Somebody will ask whether the risers are supposed to be the same. Say yes, write the question on the board next to the spread, and leave both there for a month.

Do not correct measuring technique in the first fifteen minutes. The spread has to happen honestly or the rest of the unit has nothing to work on.

title: 1.2 · Why the bubble knows
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.2 · Why the bubble knows

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why a bubble finds level and why the vial is curved.15 + 25 + 15☐ Levels ☐ Packets ☐ A clear tube if you have one
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Hand out levels. “What is actually in there, and why does it move?” Let them get to air on their own.RememberPrior knowledge · d=0.41
15–40

Air is the least dense thing in the vial, so it goes as high as the glass allows. Then the real question: why is the vial curved? A straight tube has no single high point — the bubble could sit anywhere. The curve is what turns a bubble into a reading.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “If the tube were dead straight, where would the bubble sit?”

UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
40–55Tip a level slowly and watch which way the bubble runs. Uphill, every time. Write the rule in your own words.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
FORMATIVE CHECKS“The bubble goes to the high side” is a 2. “The bubble goes to the high side BECAUSE air is lighter than the liquid, and the curve gives it one high side to go to” is a 3.
MATERIALS & PREP

Every level you can borrow — torpedo, 2-foot, 4-foot. Different vial curvatures make different sensitivities, which is a bonus conversation.

A short length of clear tube with water and an air gap makes the straight-tube case visible.

TEACHER NOTESThis is a five-dollar piece of physics that every one of them has used and none of them has been told. It costs one short session.

title: 1.3 · Two ways to find the same line
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.3 · Two ways to find the same line

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can establish plumb and level three ways and say what each instrument is referenced to.MEASURE 35 · COMPARE 40 · DRAW 35☐ Plumb bob or string + weight ☐ Levels ☐ Clear tubing ☐ Water
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Make a plumb bob: string and any weight. Hang it. It is now pointing at the centre of the earth and there is nothing you can do to it to make that untrue.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
20–55

Three instruments, one line. Plumb bob on a wall. Spirit level on the same wall. Water level between two points twenty feet apart. Do they agree? Over four feet they all agree. Over twenty feet they start to separate — and the water level is the one to believe.

Talk moves — Apply to another's reasoning: “He trusts the four-foot level. She trusts the tube. Over that distance, who is right and how would we settle it?”

EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
55–95

Draw the setup in elevation — the wall, the instrument, the reference line — dimensioned. This is the first section-type drawing in the course.

Extension: what happens to a water level if there is a bubble trapped in the tube?

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
95–110One sentence: what is a laser level referenced to, and why does that make it different from the bob?AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The closing sentence is the target. A bob is referenced to the earth. A laser is referenced to a pendulum or a gimbal INSIDE the tool, which is a thing that can be wrong.

Watch for students who think the water level works because the tube is straight. It works because water finds its own level regardless of the route.

MATERIALS & PREP

Twenty feet of clear vinyl tubing is about six dollars and it is the single best purchase in this unit. Fill it with water, tint it with a drop of food colouring so the meniscus is visible.

Two students, two ends, one bucket — practise the fill yourself first so you know how to chase the air out.

ETF covers this ground as a design task in Notebook 2.0. Here it is run backwards: you are receiving a reference line and verifying it, not inventing one.

TEACHER NOTES

If you can only buy one thing for this unit, buy the tubing. It makes “gravity is the reference” physical in a way no lecture does.

The twenty-foot comparison is where the point lands. Four feet is too short to show anything.

title: 1.4 · What a laser cannot check about itself
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.4 · What a laser cannot check about itself

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can check a level for calibration by reversing it end for end.20 + 20 + 15☐ Levels ☐ A surface that is slightly out ☐ Shims
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Set a level on a surface. Note which side of the ROOM the bubble sits. Now pick it up, turn it end for end, put it back in the same place. Where is the bubble now?ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
20–40If the bubble stayed on the same side of the room, the level is true and the surface is out. If the bubble followed the tool, the level itself is out — and half of what you read is the tool. Run the check on every level in the room.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
40–55Which of these instruments can check itself: plumb bob, spirit level, water level, laser? Argue it.EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKSThe reversal check is the assessable skill and it takes ten seconds on a job site. Watch for students who reverse the level but also move it to a different spot — that invalidates the whole check.
MATERIALS & PREP

Shim one table or board so it is genuinely out by a small amount. You want at least one surface where the answer is “the surface”.

Sabotage one level if you have a cheap one to spare — a shim under one end of the vial housing does it.

TEACHER NOTESThis is the Unit 1 instrument-check routine applied to a new tool. Say that out loud — it is the same move, not a new one.

title: 1.5 · Square is not free
bodyHtml:
SESSION 1.5 · Square is not free

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can lay out a right angle with 3-4-5 and verify a rectangle with its diagonals.LAY OUT 45 · VERIFY 30 · DRAW 35☐ Floor space ☐ Tapes ☐ Masking tape ☐ String ☐ Chalk
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15The break: plumb and level are GIVEN to you — the earth supplies them free. Square is not. Nothing in nature points at 90°. You have to build it.UnderstandClear targets · d=0.68
15–60

Lay out a rectangle on the floor with masking tape — call it 6 ft × 8 ft. No square, no framing square, nothing but tapes. Get the first corner with 3-4-5, then run the sides.

ELL/SWD: run 3-4-5 at 3-4-5 feet first as a demonstration, then scale up to 6-8-10 for the real layout.

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
60–90Now verify it — measure both diagonals. Equal means square. Record how far off you were. Then deliberately rack a second rectangle and show that all four sides are still the right length.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
90–110Draw your layout as a dimensioned plan, and put the diagonal on it as a check dimension. Trade, and have somebody verify your rectangle from your drawing alone.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Two different jobs, and students conflate them: 3-4-5 CONSTRUCTS a right angle; equal diagonals VERIFY a rectangle. Ask each crew which one they used where.

The racked rectangle is the point. Four correct side lengths and it is still wrong. That is why a tape on the sides cannot catch it.

Cycle 1 mastery records: plumb-level, bubble, level-check, square-check, 3-4-5.

MATERIALS & PREP

Clear floor — twelve by ten feet minimum. The fieldhouse floor is ideal and you were there in Unit 1.

Masking tape takes pencil and comes up clean. Chalk line if you have one.

Do NOT hand out framing squares. The whole session dies if there is a square on the table.

TEACHER NOTES

If a crew finishes early, have them lay out the same rectangle a second time using 9-12-15 and ask why that also works.

Someone will ask why 3-4-5 and not other numbers. 3² + 4² = 5² is the answer, and it is worth ten minutes if the room wants it.

CYCLE 2 — One ratio, four trades

title: 2.1 · Quarter inch per foot, on a real run
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.1 · Quarter inch per foot, on a real run

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can set and check a slope in inches per foot on a real installed run.MEASURE 45 · JUDGE 30 · DRAW 35☐ Boiler room access ☐ Levels ☐ Tapes ☐ Torpedo levels ☐ Blocks/shims
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Down to the boiler room. Find a horizontal drain or condensate run. It looks level. It is not, and it must not be.RememberPrior knowledge · d=0.41
20–65

Measure the fall on a real run. Two ways: (1) level held against the pipe, shim one end until the bubble centres, measure the shim; (2) measure the pipe height off a level reference at two points a known distance apart, subtract. Convert to inches per foot. Do both — they should agree.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Your two methods gave different numbers. Which one do you trust over eight feet, and why?”

ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
65–95Is it in code? Minimum is 1/4 inch per foot for pipe 2 1/2 inches and smaller; 1/8 inch per foot for 3 through 6 inch. Compare, decide, say by how much. This is the Unit 1 tolerance target on a new quantity.EvaluateConcept mapping · d=0.64
95–110Sketch the run in elevation with the fall called out and the two end heights dimensioned.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Two independent methods that agree is the strongest evidence a tradesman can produce, and it is the assessable move here.

Watch the unit conversion. A fall of 1 3/4 inches over 7 feet is 1/4 per foot. Students will report the 1 3/4 and stop.

MATERIALS & PREP

Clear the boiler room with facilities. Twenty students need a route and a standing spot, and you may need to split the group.

If you cannot get in: build a run on tables from 2" DWV or even cardboard tube, set it at a known fall yourself, and have them find it. Worse, but it works.

Torpedo levels are cheap and this is what they are for. Some have a 1/4-per-foot vial built in — if yours do, do not point that out until the end.

TEACHER NOTES

The pipe in your boiler room may well be out of code. That is a better lesson than a compliant one — but know the answer before class.

This is where the Unit 1 phrase “compare it to a spec and say by how much” gets its second workout on a completely different quantity.

title: 2.2 · Four trades, four units, one ratio
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.2 · Four trades, four units, one ratio

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can convert between inches per foot, pitch, percent grade and 1-in-N.15 + 25 + 15☐ Packets ☐ No calculators for the first half
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Rise over run. One triangle on the board. Then four labels for the same triangle: a plumber's 1/4 inch per foot, a carpenter's 4 in 12, an excavator's 8.3 percent, a ramp at 1:12.UnderstandWorked examples · d=0.57
15–40

The conversion table in the packet. Every row is the same slope in four costumes. Fractions by hand for the first half; calculators for the percent column.

ELL/SWD: one fully worked row in the packet with every step annotated.

ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
40–55Which trade uses which, and why does each one use the units it uses? A roofer works in twelves because a framing square has twelve inches on the tongue.AnalyzeClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKS

1/4 inch per foot is 1 in 48. If a student cannot get there, the ratio has not landed — they are pattern-matching, not proportioning.

This is the number-sense target of the unit. It is proportional reasoning with the word “proportion” never used.

MATERIALS & PREP

Nothing beyond the packet. Print the one-ratio graphic large.

A framing square on the table for the twelves conversation, if you have one.

TEACHER NOTESEvery student in this room already knows one of these four units cold and thinks the other three are a different subject. Making them the same thing is the whole session.

title: 2.3 · Too flat and too steep both clog
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.3 · Too flat and too steep both clog

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can test how slope affects what a pipe carries, and explain why there is a maximum as well as a minimum.BUILD 25 · TEST 50 · EXPLAIN 35☐ Troughs ☐ Bin/tray ☐ Water ☐ Rice or beads ☐ Blocks ☐ Tapes
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–25Build the rig: a trough on a bench, one end on blocks, a tray underneath. Set the slope by measuring rise over run and converting to inches per foot. Nobody guesses an angle — everyone sets a number.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
25–75

Run the test at 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 and 2 inches per foot. Same water, same solids, every time. Record what the water did and what the solids did SEPARATELY — that is the whole experiment.

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “At two inches per foot the water is gone in a second. So why is that a failure?”

AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
75–110Graph it: slope across the bottom, how far the solids travelled up the side. There is a window, and it has two edges. Then the sentence: too flat, nothing has the energy to move; too steep, the water outruns the solids and leaves them stranded on the pipe wall.EvaluateConcept mapping · d=0.64
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The two failure modes have to be described DIFFERENTLY. A student who says “it clogs” at both ends has not got it.

The graph is the Reasoning evidence. A curve with a peak, not a straight line.

This is the physics target of the unit and it is genuinely falsifiable — their rig can disagree with the claim.

MATERIALS & PREP

TROUGH: split 2" PVC or vinyl gutter is ideal (about $8 for ten feet). Cardboard folded into a V and lined with a strip of plastic sheet or a cut-open bag works and costs nothing. Make four to six so crews run in parallel.

SOLIDS: rice, dry beans, or paper pellets. Anything that sinks and does not dissolve.

IF YOU CANNOT USE WATER IN YOUR ROOM: run it dry with sand and beads. You will get the too-flat end honestly and the too-steep end only partly — say so out loud rather than pretending the model is complete.

Towels. A tray or bin under every trough. This is the messiest session in the course and it is worth it.

TEACHER NOTES

Code gives you the minimum. The maximum is not in the code — it is physics, and nobody writes it on a print. That gap is the point of the session.

Real pipe has a wall that solids drag on; a smooth trough is kinder than the real thing. Name that limitation of the model rather than hiding it.

title: 2.4 · What the fall costs you
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.4 · What the fall costs you

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can work out the total fall over a run and say what it costs in depth.15 + 25 + 15☐ Packets ☐ No calculators
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Twenty-two feet at a quarter inch per foot. How much does the pipe drop end to end? Do it before anybody says a number out loud.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
15–40Five runs in the packet, five answers. Then the second column: where does that fall come from? A 5 1/2 inch drop inside a 9 1/4 inch joist bay leaves you very little, and the conduit is already in there.AnalyzeWorked examples · d=0.57
40–55The reverse question, which is the one that comes up on a job: “I have 4 inches of depth to play with. How long a run can I get?”EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
FORMATIVE CHECKS

The reverse question separates students who can run the proportion from students who memorised one multiplication.

22 × 1/4 = 5 1/2. Fractions, by hand. If they reach for a calculator for that, the Unit 1 fraction work needs revisiting.

MATERIALS & PREPNothing beyond the packet. Actual joist depths on the board: 2×8 is 7 1/4, 2×10 is 9 1/4, 2×12 is 11 1/4.
TEACHER NOTESThis is the arithmetic that makes 3.3 and 3.5 possible. Do not skip it if the week runs short — drop 3.2 instead.

title: 2.5 · Draw the fall
bodyHtml:
SESSION 2.5 · Draw the fall

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can draw a sloped run in plan and in section with the fall called out correctly.DRAW 70 · HAND IT OVER 40☐ Straightedges ☐ Rules ☐ Paper ☐ Scale reference page
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–30A plan shows you where. A section shows you how deep. A slope is invisible in plan — which is why it gets called out in a note and dimensioned in section. Both, for the same run.UnderstandWorked examples · d=0.57
30–80

Draw the run you measured in the boiler room, to a stated scale: plan with the fall noted, section with both end elevations dimensioned. Every Unit 1 dimensioning rule still applies.

Extension: add a second fixture branching in partway along and dimension where it ties in.

ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
80–110Trade. The reader has to state, from the drawing alone, the fall per foot and the elevation at both ends. If they cannot, something is missing.EvaluatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Two things go wrong and both are worth catching: fall drawn but never called out in a note, and fall called out but the section not actually drawn to it.

Cycle 2 mastery records: slope-set, rise-run, slope-why, fall-total, plan-and-section.

MATERIALS & PREP

Straightedges. This is a drafting session, not a sketching one.

Post the Unit 1 dimensioning reference page again. It is still the standard.

TEACHER NOTESSEQUENCING NOTE: section drawing is introduced here rather than in Unit 3. The reasoning is that you should be able to draw a section before you are asked to draw forces on one. If you would rather it live in Unit 3, this session becomes elevation-only and Unit 3 picks up sections with load arrows.

CYCLE 3 — Where it collides

title: 3.1 · Why it is always the first riser and the last
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.1 · Why it is always the first riser and the last

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why the end risers in a flight are the ones that end up wrong, and compare a spread to a code tolerance.RESOLVE 30 · MEASURE 45 · EXPLAIN 35☐ Stair access ☐ Tapes ☐ 1.1 data ☐ Board
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15A month ago you measured every riser in that flight and the biggest and smallest did not match. The number is still in the box on the board. Today we find out what it means.RememberSpaced retrieval · d=0.65
15–45

The code: the greatest riser height in a flight may not exceed the smallest by more than 3/8 of an inch. Same for treads. Compare your spread. Does this school's stair pass?

Talk moves — Press for reasoning: “Why would a code care about consistency instead of just setting a maximum height?”

EvaluateConcept mapping · d=0.64
45–85Back to the stair. WHERE in the flight is the error? Almost always the first riser, the last, or both. The stringer was cut for equal risers — then finish floor went down at one end and not the other, and the whole error landed on the two risers nobody re-measured. Go and measure the finish floor thickness at top and bottom and see whether it accounts for the miss.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
85–110Write the explanation. Not “it is off” — WHY it is off, WHERE the error went, and what would have prevented it.CreateFeedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

This is the payoff of 1.1 and the best Reasoning target in the unit. Score the explanation, not the measurement.

The connection to Unit 1 is exact: a chain of equal risers laid out from one end, with an unaccounted thickness at the datum. Say it in those words and watch who recognises it.

Cycle 3 begins. The tolerance target is the same one from Unit 1, now against a published code number rather than a spec you invented.

MATERIALS & PREP

Know the answer before class. Measure the finish floor thickness at both landings yourself.

IF THE FLIGHT PASSES CLEANLY, that is a real result and you use it: somebody accounted for the finish floor at layout, and you can ask what they must have done differently.

Code reference: IRC R311.7.5.1 for the 3/8 inch limit, same in IBC. Have the actual text if you can — students take a printed code page more seriously than a teacher's number.

TEACHER NOTES

Trip incidents on stairs cluster at the top and bottom step. That is not a coincidence and it is worth one minute, not ten.

Do not let this become a lecture about code. The code number is the tolerance; the physics is the accumulation.

title: 3.2 · Rack it
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.2 · Rack it

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can explain why a rectangle racks and a triangle does not, and say where a brace belongs.20 + 20 + 15☐ Cardboard strips ☐ Paper fasteners or tape ☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20Build a four-bar rectangle from cardboard strips with pinned corners. Push it. Now add one diagonal. Push it again.ApplyWorked examples · d=0.57
20–40Why? A triangle's shape is fixed by its three side lengths alone — there is only one triangle with those sides. A rectangle's is not. That is the entire reason for sheathing, a let-in brace, a gusset, and the diagonal in a gate.UnderstandVocabulary/inductive · d=0.67
40–55Back to 1.5: you verified square with the diagonals. Now you know why the diagonal is the dimension that carries the information.AnalyzeConcept mapping · d=0.64
FORMATIVE CHECKSConnecting the brace to the diagonal check is the target. Same line, two jobs — one measures the shape, one holds it.
MATERIALS & PREP

Cardboard strips and brass fasteners. Tape works but pivots badly.

One real example on the board: a gate that sags, a shear wall, a knee brace.

TEACHER NOTESYour carpenters will already know a brace goes in. None of them will have connected it to the diagonal they measure for square.

title: 3.3 · The bay is already full
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.3 · The bay is already full

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can read a bay section and say which service has to move, and why.READ 35 · ROUTE 40 · ARGUE 35☐ Bay section handout ☐ Straightedges ☐ Rules ☐ Packets
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–35One joist bay, three trades. The conduit is level and it got there first. The drain has to fall a quarter inch per foot. The joist can only be bored in its middle third. Read the section and find the collision.AnalyzeFormative assessment · d=0.68
35–75

Route the drain. It will not fit as drawn. Your options are the real ones: deepen the joist, drop a soffit, move the conduit, move the fixture, or reduce the fall. Cost each one out in inches, not in opinions.

Talk moves — Apply to another's reasoning: “He says move the conduit. She says drop the ceiling. Which one costs the owner more, and how would you know?”

EvaluateClassroom discussion · d=0.82
75–110Nobody in this drawing is wrong. Write the case for the trade you were assigned — not the trade you are in. Then hear the other two.CreatePeer feedback · d=0.70
FORMATIVE CHECKS

“Reduce the fall” is the answer that fails silently and it is the one to watch for. It works on the drawing and it clogs in two years. A student who names it AND rejects it with a reason is scoring a 4.

Assign trades deliberately, and not the student's own. Arguing the other trade's case is the Transfer target.

MATERIALS & PREP

Draw the bay section handout at a stated scale so they can measure off it. The graphic in the packet is the teaching version; they need one they can work on.

Real numbers make it real: 2×10 joist is 9 1/4 deep, middle third is roughly the middle 3 inches, 2" DWV is 2 3/8 outside.

This is ETF's design loop territory, run backwards. They are not designing the bay; they are receiving it, finding the conflict, and defending a resolution.

TEACHER NOTES

This is the cross-trade collision of the unit. Every student meets a constraint that belongs to somebody else's trade.

Boring and notching limits get named here but not derived — that is Unit 3, and it needs load first. Park it out loud.

title: 3.4 · Call the fall
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.4 · Call the fall

SHORT ~55 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can estimate a slope by eye and then check myself.15 + 25 + 15☐ Levels ☐ Tapes ☐ Anything sloped in the building
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–15Estimation call. Look at a run — a ramp, a gutter, a pipe, a parking lot — and write down your guess in inches per foot BEFORE you measure. Everybody commits on paper.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
15–40Now measure it. High minus low, divided by the run. How close were you? Do it five times on five different things and watch your guesses get better.AnalyzeSpaced retrieval · d=0.65
40–55Marzano self-rating on the Cycle 3 targets.EvaluateMetacognitive self-assessment · d=0.60
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Calling it before measuring is the habit worth building — it is what makes a measurement a check instead of a discovery.

Track improvement across the five calls, not accuracy on any one.

MATERIALS & PREP

Scout five sloped things in the building in advance: a ramp, an exterior walk, a gutter, a boiler-room pipe, a drain in a floor slab.

The ADA ramp, if you have one, should be 1:12 or flatter. That is a checkable claim.

TEACHER NOTESShort and cheap and it moves. Use it as the recovery session if a week goes short — but do not cut 2.4 for it.

title: 3.5 · Mastery task — route it and prove the fall
bodyHtml:
SESSION 3.5 · Mastery task — route it and prove the fall

LONG SESSION ~110 min

TARGETSHAPEMATERIALS READY?I can route a run, prove the fall fits, and show what it costs the framing — or show that it cannot be done.WALK 20 · READ 15 · SOLVE 40 · DRAW 35☐ Task sheet ☐ Bay section, to scale ☐ Instruments ☐ Rubric posted
TIMEWHAT HAPPENSBLOOM’SHATTIE
0–20

THE WALK. No task sheet yet. They look at a real bay — exposed ceiling, boiler room, anywhere services are visible — and fill in the scope sheet from what is in front of them.

The one place in the course where they decide what the job is instead of receiving it. Nothing gets handed out until the sheets are in.

AnalyzeClear targets · d=0.68
20–35NOW hand out the task: a bay section, a fixture location, and a point of connection. Read the four scoring dimensions aloud.UnderstandClear targets · d=0.68
35–75Work it. Total fall over the run. Does it clear the conduit? Does the bore land in the middle third? Is the fall still in code at both ends? Every claim gets a number beside it.ApplyFormative assessment · d=0.68
75–110Produce the drawing: plan with the fall called out, section with both end elevations and the bore located, scale stated. Then the written finding — it fits and here is the proof, or it does not fit and here is exactly what has to change and by how much. Self-score before handing in.CreateMetacognitive self-assessment · d=0.60
FORMATIVE CHECKS

Score all four dimensions. Grade is the lowest, never the average.

The walk sheet is scored too, and it is where HS-ETS1-1 lives. Line 5 — what code says — is the societal requirement the standard asks for, and here it has an actual number.

The drawing carries Communication. The fall arithmetic carries Science. The resolution argument carries Reasoning. Naming what it costs another trade carries Transfer.

Make two versions with different run lengths so neighbours cannot copy an answer.
